docs.title: DDM Documentation
docs.text:
DDM (Data Donation Module) is an open-source web application for collecting data donations for academic research. In a data donation, participants request a copy of the data that a platform such as YouTube or Instagram has collected about them, and share selected parts of it with researchers.

DDM is developed and maintained by the Data Donation Lab at the University of Zurich.

docs.title: Documentation Structure
docs.text:
• For Researchers: Set up and run data donation projects on an existing DDM server.
  • For System Administrators: Install and run a DDM server.
  • For Developers: Contribute to DDM, or fork and extend it.

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
• Easy data donation configuration

    Researchers can configure the data donation collection (including validation and extraction), access collected data, and monitor ongoing data collections through a graphical user interface.

    Project configurations can also easily be shared through the integrated export-import functionality.

  • Supports many platforms

    Collect data donations from all platforms that provide a text-based data export, including:

    • YouTube
    • TikTok
    • Instagram
    • ChatGPT

  • Integrated survey tool

    DDM includes a built-in, modern survey tool supporting the most used survey functionality.

    Furthermore, DDM can also easily be connected to your survey projects hosted on other platforms (Qualtrics, Unipark, SoSci Survey, etc.).

  • Privacy by design

    DDM puts participant privacy first.

    Local Processing: Donated data is extracted in the participant's browser and only submitted after explicit consent.

    Encryption: All donated data is encrypted before storage.

    Enhanced Encryption: Encrypt a project's data with a password that only your team knows, so that not even the server administrators can read it (e.g., if you're dealing with health data).

docs.title: How a Data Donation Works
docs.text:
Participants go through these steps:

  1. Briefing page: Participants learn about the study.
  2. Data donation:
    1. Participants follow the instructions to request their data from the platform and download it.
    2. They upload the file to DDM.
    3. DDM extracts and filters the data according to the researcher's rules, in the participant's browser.
    4. Participants review the extracted data and decide whether to donate it.
  3. Questionnaire (optional): Participants answer questions, which can refer to their donated data, for example to add context or to show participants insights into their own data.
  4. Debriefing page: The last page, which can send participants on to another website, such as an external survey.

The content of a donation is sent to the researcher's server only after the participant consents in step 2.4. For details, see Data Donation Overview.

docs.title: Design Philosophy
docs.text:
DDM is designed to be hosted by an institution, such as a university, a department, or a research consortium, and to run many independent data donation projects at the same time. It also works for a single project.

Researchers configure everything in a graphical user interface, without programming.

For more on DDM's design, see the accompanying article.

docs.text:

  author  = {Pfiffner, Nico and Witlox, Pim and Friemel, Thomas N.},

docs.title: Reporting Issues
docs.text:
If you encounter issues or detect a bug, please open a new issue in the GitHub repository.

If you need help navigating the application, please first look for a solution in the sections of this documentation. If you are stuck and don't find what you are looking for, feel free to contact us at datadonation@ikmz.uzh.ch.

docs.title: System Administrators
docs.text: Use this section to set up and maintain a server that hosts DDM data donation projects, either for yourself or for your institution.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
DDM is a Django app, not a standalone server: it runs inside a Django project that you host. You need:

  • A server that can run a Python/Django application.
  • A database. SQLite works for testing; use PostgreSQL or MariaDB in production.
  • Optional: Access to an OpenID Connect (OIDC) provider, if researchers should log in with their institutional account. See User Authentication.

docs.title: In this section
docs.text:
• Installation Guide: Install DDM and get it running.
  • Configuration: Set up user authentication and customize admin templates and the CKEditor text editor.
  • Settings Reference: Look up all available DDM settings.
  • Security: Secure your DDM installation.

docs.title: Installation Guide
docs.text:
DDM is a Django app. To run it, you need Python 3.12 or newer (download) and a Django 5.2 project to install DDM into. This guide walks you through creating that project and adding DDM to it:

  1. Create a Django project.
  2. Configure the database.
  3. Install DDM and configure your project for it.
  4. Set up the database tables.
  5. Test the installation.
  6. Prepare for production.

For a production deployment (for example, with PostgreSQL, Nginx, and Gunicorn), follow a comprehensive guide such as How To Set Up Django with Postgres, Nginx, and Gunicorn alongside this one.

docs.title: Create a Django Project
docs.text:
Create a virtual environment and install Django into it. The commands below use venv and pip on Linux or macOS. For Windows, see the Python venv documentation.

python -m venv /path/to/venv
source /path/to/venv/bin/activate
pip install "Django>=5.2,<6"

Using uv instead

uv is faster and manages the virtual environment for you:

    uv init --app
    uv add "Django>=5.2,<6"

For the rest of this guide, prefix commands with uv run instead of activating the environment (for example, uv run django-admin startproject yourproject or uv run python manage.py migrate), and install DDM with uv add django-ddm instead of pip install django-ddm.

Create a new project and change into its folder:

django-admin startproject yourproject
cd yourproject

The yourproject folder contains manage.py and a subfolder, also named yourproject, that holds settings.py and urls.py.

To check that Django works, start the development server and open http://127.0.0.1:8000:

python manage.py runserver

docs.title: Configure the Database
docs.text: New Django projects use SQLite, which is fine for development. For production, use PostgreSQL or MariaDB: install the database server and its Python driver, then update DATABASES in settings.py. See Get your database running and the DATABASES reference.

docs.title: Install DDM
docs.text:
Install the DDM package. pip installs its dependencies automatically.

pip install django-ddm

Then update your project's settings.py and urls.py as described below.

docs.title: Update settings.py
docs.text:
Installed apps. Add DDM and its dependencies to INSTALLED_APPS:

# settings.py

INSTALLED_APPS = [
    # ...
    'ddm',
    'ddm.auth',
    'ddm.logging',
    'ddm.questionnaire',
    'ddm.datadonation',
    'ddm.participation',
    'ddm.projects',
    'ddm.core',
    'django_ckeditor_5',
    'webpack_loader',
    'rest_framework',
    'rest_framework.authtoken',
]

App order matters if you customize templates

If you override DDM templates (see Template Customization), list the app that contains your overrides before ddm.core. Django's template loader searches INSTALLED_APPS in order and uses the first match.

Static files and webpack-loader. DDM's frontend ships as pre-built bundles that collectstatic copies into STATIC_ROOT. If your settings don't define STATIC_ROOT yet, add it:

# settings.py

STATIC_ROOT = BASE_DIR / 'static'

Then add the webpack-loader configuration as-is:

# settings.py
import os

WEBPACK_LOADER = {
    'DDM_UPLOADER': {
        'CACHE': True,
        'BUNDLE_DIR_NAME': 'ddm_core/frontend/uploader/',
        'STATS_FILE': os.path.join(STATIC_ROOT, 'ddm_core/frontend/uploader/webpack-stats.json'),
        'POLL_INTERVAL': 0.1,
        'IGNORE': [r'.+\.hot-update.js', r'.+\.map'],
    },
    'DDM_QUESTIONNAIRE': {
        'CACHE': True,
        'BUNDLE_DIR_NAME': 'ddm_core/frontend/questionnaire/',
        'STATS_FILE': os.path.join(STATIC_ROOT, 'ddm_core/frontend/questionnaire/webpack-stats.json'),
        'POLL_INTERVAL': 0.1,
        'TIMEOUT': None,
        'IGNORE': [r'.+\.hot-update.js', r'.+\.map'],
    },
}

Context processor. Add the DDM context processor. It shows the installed DDM version below the header of the researcher interface:

# settings.py

TEMPLATES = [
    {
        # ...
        'OPTIONS': {
            'context_processors': [
                # ...
                'ddm.core.context_processors.add_ddm_version',
            ],
        },
    },
]

Login redirects. Set where users go after logging in and out. Without LOGIN_REDIRECT_URL, Django sends users to /accounts/profile/, which doesn't exist:

# settings.py

LOGIN_REDIRECT_URL = '/ddm/projects/'
LOGOUT_REDIRECT_URL = '/login/'

CKEditor uploads. Allow researchers to upload images in instructions and question texts, and limit the file size:

# settings.py

CKEDITOR_5_FILE_UPLOAD_PERMISSION = 'authenticated'
CKEDITOR_5_MAX_FILE_SIZE = 10  # In MB. The default, 0, means unlimited.

Allowing PDFs and videos

To also allow other file types, set CKEDITOR_5_ALLOW_ALL_FILE_TYPES = True and list them in CKEDITOR_5_UPLOAD_FILE_TYPES (for example, ['jpeg', 'png', 'pdf', 'mp4']). DDM then checks only the file extension, not the content, and any logged-in user can upload. Read Security → CKEditor File Upload Security first.

For all CKEditor options, see the django-ckeditor-5 documentation.

Media files. CKEditor stores uploaded files in Django's media storage. Set where to store them and the URL to serve them from:

# settings.py

MEDIA_ROOT = BASE_DIR / 'media'
MEDIA_URL = '/media/'

Time zone support. DDM requires USE_TZ = True. New Django projects set this by default; if you're adding DDM to an existing project, check it:

# settings.py

USE_TZ = True

DDM settings (optional). Use DDM_SETTINGS to restrict who can create projects by email pattern, or to adjust upload size and API rate limits:

# settings.py

DDM_SETTINGS = {
    'EMAIL_PERMISSION_CHECK': r'.*(\.|@)somedomain\.com$',
}

For all DDM settings and their defaults, see Settings Reference.

docs.title: Update urls.py
docs.text:
Add the DDM, login, logout, and CKEditor upload endpoints to your project's urls.py:

# urls.py
from django.contrib.auth import views as auth_views
from django.urls import path, include

urlpatterns = [
    # ...
    path('ddm/', include('ddm.core.urls')),
    path('login/', auth_views.LoginView.as_view(template_name='ddm_auth/login.html'), name='ddm_login'),
    path('logout/', auth_views.LogoutView.as_view(), name='ddm_logout'),
    path('ckeditor5/', include('django_ckeditor_5.urls')),
]

The ddm_auth/login.html template shows a password login form. To let researchers log in through your institution instead, see User Authentication.

To serve uploaded files during development, also add:

# urls.py
from django.conf import settings
from django.conf.urls.static import static

if settings.DEBUG:
    urlpatterns += static(settings.MEDIA_URL, document_root=settings.MEDIA_ROOT)

Using DDM alongside Wagtail

If your site also runs Wagtail with internationalized URLs, set prefix_default_language=False in i18n_patterns. Otherwise, Wagtail's URL patterns can shadow DDM's:

    # urls.py
    from django.conf.urls.i18n import i18n_patterns
    from django.urls import path, include
    from wagtail import urls as wagtail_urls

    urlpatterns += i18n_patterns(
        path('', include(wagtail_urls)),
        prefix_default_language=False,
    )

docs.title: Set Up the Database Tables
docs.text:
Create the database tables and a superuser account:

python manage.py migrate
python manage.py createsuperuser

docs.title: Test the Installation
docs.text:
Collect static files (required for the webpack-loader configuration) and start the server:

python manage.py collectstatic
python manage.py runserver

Then check both interfaces:

  • http://127.0.0.1:8000/admin: Log in as the superuser and confirm that DDM appears in the Django admin site.
  • http://127.0.0.1:8000/ddm/projects: Confirm that the project overview loads and that you can create a project.

docs.title: Prepare for Production
docs.text:
Before you expose your installation to the internet:

  • Harden Django. New projects default to DEBUG = True and leave Django's other production settings (secure cookies, SSL redirect, HSTS) unset. Set DEBUG = False and run Django's deployment check:
    python manage.py check --deploy

See the
[Django deployment checklist](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/stable/howto/deployment/checklist/)
for what each check covers.
  • Serve static and media files. With DEBUG = False, Django no longer serves static or uploaded files. Configure your web server (for example, Nginx) to serve STATIC_ROOT at STATIC_URL and MEDIA_ROOT at MEDIA_URL. See Deploying static files.
  • Work through the DDM security checklist. DDM uses SECRET_KEY to encrypt donated data, so losing or leaking it has consequences beyond a typical Django site. See the Security checklist before you generate and store it.
  • Throttle login attempts. Django's login view has no brute-force protection. If you keep local password login (instead of only OIDC login), add throttling yourself, for example with django-axes.

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• Configuration: Set up institutional login, customize templates, and adjust the CKEditor toolbar.
  • Settings Reference: Look up all DDM settings, for example default header images for participation pages.
  • Security: Review security considerations for running DDM.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: This page covers the security considerations that are specific to DDM. For general Django hardening, see Installation Guide → Prepare for Production.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• Back up SECRET_KEY and keep it out of version control. See Secret Key & Encryption at Rest.
  • Restrict researcher access with EMAIL_PERMISSION_CHECK. See Access & Login.
  • If you use local password login, throttle login attempts. See Access & Login.
  • Set an upload size limit and review the allowed file types. See File Uploads.
  • Set a Content Security Policy. See Content Security Policy.

docs.title: Secret Key & Encryption at Rest
docs.text:
In DDM, SECRET_KEY is part of the encryption key for donated data. DDM uses it to derive the key that protects each project's private key (see Developers → Encryption for details). This applies to all standard projects; projects with enhanced encryption are not affected (see below).

This has two consequences:

  • If you lose SECRET_KEY, you lose the data. Without it, donated data in standard projects can't be decrypted. Changing SECRET_KEY has the same effect: DDM has no way to re-encrypt existing projects with a new key. Back up SECRET_KEY as carefully as your database.
  • If SECRET_KEY leaks, the data is exposed. Anyone with SECRET_KEY and access to your database can decrypt all donated data in standard projects. Keep it out of version control, load it from an environment variable or a secrets manager, and don't reuse it across deployments.

Enhanced encryption. Projects with enhanced encryption derive their key from a project-specific passphrase that DDM never stores. SECRET_KEY doesn't affect them.

docs.title: If Your Secret Key Leaks
docs.text:
1. Export the donated data of all standard projects. After the next step, DDM can no longer decrypt it.
  2. Generate a new SECRET_KEY and deploy it.
  3. Back up the new key.

docs.title: Access & Login
docs.text:
Restrict researcher access. Any logged-in user whose email matches DDM_SETTINGS['EMAIL_PERMISSION_CHECK'] gets researcher access. If the setting isn't defined, every logged-in user does, including everyone your OIDC provider authenticates. See User Authentication → Access Control.

Throttle login attempts. Django's login view has no brute-force protection. If you keep local password login (instead of only OIDC login), add throttling yourself, for example with django-axes.

Multi-factor authentication. DDM doesn't provide MFA for local password login. To require it, enforce it at your OIDC provider (recommended) or add a third-party Django MFA package.

docs.title: CKEditor File Upload Security
docs.text:
Researchers can upload files in the rich text editor. These settings control uploads (see Settings Reference for defaults):

  • CKEDITOR_5_FILE_UPLOAD_PERMISSION
  • CKEDITOR_5_ALLOW_ALL_FILE_TYPES
  • CKEDITOR_5_UPLOAD_FILE_TYPES
  • CKEDITOR_5_MAX_FILE_SIZE

With CKEDITOR_5_FILE_UPLOAD_PERMISSION = 'authenticated', every logged-in user can upload files, not only users with researcher access. Control who can log in, for example through your OIDC provider.

docs.title: Risk: Allowing All File Types
docs.text:
By default (CKEDITOR_5_ALLOW_ALL_FILE_TYPES = False), only images can be uploaded, and their content is validated.

With CKEDITOR_5_ALLOW_ALL_FILE_TYPES = True, only the file extension is checked, not the content. As a result:

  • Malicious files can use an allowed extension (for example, malware.pdf).
  • Polyglot files (valid as two file types at once) can pass the extension check.
  • PDFs can contain JavaScript or exploits.

docs.title: Mitigations
docs.text:
Always set an upload size limit. CKEDITOR_5_MAX_FILE_SIZE defaults to 0 (unlimited), so any logged-in user can fill your disk:

# settings.py

CKEDITOR_5_MAX_FILE_SIZE = 10  # In MB.

If users you don't fully trust can log in, also consider:

Mitigation How Restrict file types If you don't need PDFs, keep CKEDITOR_5_ALLOW_ALL_FILE_TYPES = False. Sanitize PDFs If you need PDFs, strip JavaScript and embedded content with a sanitization library. Validate content Check each file's magic bytes to confirm that its content matches its extension. Set secure headers Serve uploads with Content-Disposition: attachment and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff. Isolate domains Serve uploads from a separate domain so that uploaded files can't access session cookies.

docs.title: Content Security Policy
docs.text:
All DDM pages work under a strict Content Security Policy (CSP) without exceptions, for example:

default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; style-src 'self'

To set a CSP on your deployment, use django-csp or your web server.

docs.title: Rate Limiting
docs.text:
DDM limits the request rate on the two endpoints that clients can reach without a researcher login. For the settings and their format, see Settings Reference.

Endpoint Default limit Project API (token-authenticated; see Researchers → APIs) 100 requests/minute per token Client-side exception log (public; see Researchers → Project Logs) 20 requests/minute per IP address

Researchers who are logged in to the researcher interface aren't rate-limited.

docs.title: Settings Reference
docs.text:
This page lists the settings that configure DDM in your project's settings.py:

  • DDM Settings: DDM's own settings. All are optional.
  • Django and Third-Party Settings: Settings of Django and the packages DDM uses, with the values DDM needs.

Researchers configure per-project options, such as branding, in the researcher interface; see For Researchers.

docs.title: DDM_SETTINGS
docs.text:
A dictionary of DDM's own settings. All keys are optional; if you omit the dictionary, DDM uses the defaults.

Key Default Description EMAIL_PERMISSION_CHECK Not set (no restriction) Regular expression, matched against the start of the email address. Only users whose email matches get researcher access; anchor the pattern with $ to also require a match at the end, as in the example below. Superusers and users with Ignore email restriction enabled always get access. See User Authentication. MAX_DONATION_UPLOAD_SIZE 104857600 (100 MB) Maximum size in bytes of the uncompressed data_donation.json in a participant's upload. Larger uploads are rejected and logged. PROJECT_API_THROTTLE_RATE '100/min' Rate limit per access token for the project API. See Security → Rate Limiting. EXCEPTION_LOG_THROTTLE_RATE '20/min' Rate limit per IP address for the public client-side exception log. See Security → Rate Limiting.

Rate limits use the format '<number>/<period>', where the period is s, min, h, or d (for example, '200/min').

# settings.py

DDM_SETTINGS = {
    'EMAIL_PERMISSION_CHECK': r'.*(\.|@)somedomain\.com$',
    'MAX_DONATION_UPLOAD_SIZE': 100 * 1024 * 1024,
    'PROJECT_API_THROTTLE_RATE': '100/min',
    'EXCEPTION_LOG_THROTTLE_RATE': '20/min',
}

docs.title: Header Images
docs.text:
Default images for the header of the participant-facing pages. Researchers can replace them per project.

Setting Default Description DDM_DEFAULT_HEADER_IMG_LEFT '' (no image) URL of the image on the left side of the header. DDM_DEFAULT_HEADER_IMG_RIGHT '' (no image) URL of the image on the right side of the header.

Use a URL the browser can load: either a full URL or a path your server serves, such as a file under STATIC_URL.

# settings.py

DDM_DEFAULT_HEADER_IMG_LEFT = '/static/images/logo_left.png'
DDM_DEFAULT_HEADER_IMG_RIGHT = 'https://example.org/logo_right.png'

docs.title: Django and Third-Party Settings
docs.text: These settings belong to Django or to packages DDM depends on. The tables list only the settings that matter for DDM, with the values DDM needs or recommends. The Installation Guide shows how to set them.

docs.title: Django
docs.text:
Setting Value for DDM Description SECRET_KEY Required; keep secret and back it up Part of the encryption key for donated data in standard projects. Losing or changing it makes that data unreadable. See Security → Secret Key & Encryption at Rest. USE_TZ True (required) Enables time zone support. New projects set this by default. STATIC_ROOT Required, for example BASE_DIR / 'static' Where collectstatic puts static files, including DDM's frontend bundles. MEDIA_ROOT Required, for example BASE_DIR / 'media' Where files uploaded through CKEditor are stored. MEDIA_URL Required, for example '/media/' URL that uploaded files are served from. LOGIN_REDIRECT_URL Recommended: '/ddm/projects/' Where users go after logging in. Django's default, '/accounts/profile/', doesn't exist in DDM. LOGOUT_REDIRECT_URL Recommended: '/login/' Where users go after logging out. Django's default is None.

For login views and OIDC setup, see User Authentication.

docs.title: CKEditor
docs.text:
Settings of django-ckeditor-5, the rich text editor that DDM uses. See Security → CKEditor File Upload Security before you change the upload settings.

Setting Default Description CKEDITOR_5_CONFIGS DDM's ddm_ckeditor and ddm_ckeditor_temp_func configurations Editor configurations. If you define ddm_ckeditor or ddm_ckeditor_temp_func, your version replaces DDM's. See CKEditor Configuration. CKEDITOR_5_FILE_UPLOAD_PERMISSION 'staff' Who can upload files. Set it to 'authenticated' so researchers who aren't staff can upload. CKEDITOR_5_ALLOW_ALL_FILE_TYPES False If False, only images are accepted, and their content is validated. If True, only the extension is checked. CKEDITOR_5_UPLOAD_FILE_TYPES ['jpg', 'jpeg', 'png', 'gif', 'bmp', 'webp', 'tiff'] Allowed file extensions if CKEDITOR_5_ALLOW_ALL_FILE_TYPES = True. CKEDITOR_5_MAX_FILE_SIZE 0 (unlimited) Maximum upload size in MB. Always set a limit.

docs.title: webpack-loader
docs.text: Setting Value for DDM Description WEBPACK_LOADER Required; copy the configuration from the Installation Guide Points django-webpack-loader to DDM's pre-built frontend bundles (DDM_UPLOADER and DDM_QUESTIONNAIRE).

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
These guides cover common ways to adapt DDM to your institution after installation:

  • User Authentication: Let researchers log in with their institutional account through OpenID Connect (OIDC).
  • Template Customization: Override DDM's templates to change the look of the researcher interface.
  • CKEditor Configuration: Change the editor toolbar that researchers use for instructions and question texts.

For a complete list of available settings, see Settings Reference.

docs.title: Override the Configurations
docs.text:
Each CKEditor configuration defines what researchers can do in the editor, for example which toolbar buttons and formatting options are available. If the defaults don't fit your needs, such as when you want to remove the option to embed media or add a table tool, you can override them.

To do so, define the configuration in CKEDITOR_5_CONFIGS in settings.py. Your configuration replaces DDM's default for that editor entirely; any editor you don't define keeps its default.

The simplest way is to copy DDM's default from ddm/core/ckeditor_config.py and change only what you need:

# settings.py

CKEDITOR_5_CONFIGS = {
    'ddm_ckeditor': {
        # Copy of DDM's default, with your changes.
    },
}

Warning

If you override ddm_ckeditor_temp_func, keep support for the <template-func> element. Otherwise, researchers can't add dynamic content to their questions.

For available options, see the django-ckeditor-5 documentation and the CKEditor 5 documentation.

docs.title: Template Customization
docs.text: The researcher interface has a minimal header and footer without account options such as a logout button, because your Django project handles authentication (see User Authentication). To add your own branding or account options, override DDM's base template using Django's template inheritance.

docs.title: Override the Header and Footer
docs.text:
1. In one of your apps, create the file your_app/templates/ddm_core/base.html.
  2. Extend DDM's base template and override the blocks you want to change: 
        {% extends "ddm_core/base.html" %}

    {% block extrahead %}
        {{ block.super }}
        <!-- Custom CSS, favicon, etc. -->
    {% endblock %}

    {% block header %}
    <div>
        <!-- Your header HTML -->
        <form method="post" action="{% url 'ddm_logout' %}">
            {% csrf_token %}
            <button type="submit">Log out</button>
        </form>
    </div>
    {% endblock %}

    {% block footer %}
    <div>
        <!-- Your footer HTML -->
    </div>
    {% endblock %}

Use {{ block.super }} to keep DDM's default content of a block and add to it. Django's logout view only accepts POST requests, so use a form for the logout button, not a link.

  1. Make sure your app comes before ddm.core in INSTALLED_APPS.

Overrides are ignored if the app order is wrong

Django's template loader searches INSTALLED_APPS in order and uses the first match. If your app comes after ddm.core, Django uses DDM's own ddm_core/base.html and silently ignores your override. See Installation Guide → Update settings.py.

docs.title: Available Blocks
docs.text:
ddm_core/base.html defines the following blocks:

Block Contains extrahead Extra content for <head>, such as CSS or a favicon. page_title The page title. header The page header. main_heading_wrapper The page heading; wraps main_heading and sub_heading. pre_footer The area above the footer; wraps pre_footer_left and pre_footer_right. footer The page footer. scripts Extra <script> tags at the end of <body>.

docs.title: User Authentication
docs.text:
DDM uses Django's built-in user management. Researchers log in with a Django user account, either with a local password or through your institution's login. The Installation Guide sets up local password login; this page explains who gets researcher access and how to add institutional login.

For institutional deployments, we recommend login through OpenID Connect (OIDC); see Set Up OIDC Login. If you run DDM only for yourself or a few trusted users, local password login is enough.

docs.title: Access Control
docs.text:
There's no separate registration for DDM. When a logged-in user opens a researcher page for the first time, DDM creates a research profile for them automatically. DDM then grants access if one of the following is true:

  • The user is a superuser.
  • The user's email address matches DDM_SETTINGS['EMAIL_PERMISSION_CHECK'].
  • The user's research profile has Ignore email restriction enabled.
  • EMAIL_PERMISSION_CHECK isn't set.

Users without access see a "no permission" page instead of the project list.

Set an email restriction

If you don't set EMAIL_PERMISSION_CHECK, every user who can log in gets researcher access. With OIDC, that includes everyone your provider authenticates, because mozilla-django-oidc creates accounts automatically on first login. See Settings Reference.

docs.title: Grant Access to an Individual User
docs.text:
To give access to someone whose email doesn't match the restriction (for example, an external collaborator):

  1. Open the Django admin site (/admin/) and log in as a superuser.
  2. Open the user's research profile.
  3. Enable Ignore email restriction and save.

docs.title: Set Up OIDC Login
docs.text:
We recommend mozilla-django-oidc for OIDC login. The steps below cover the basic setup; for all options, see the mozilla-django-oidc documentation.

  1. Register a client with your OIDC provider. Use https://<your-domain>/oidc/callback/ as the redirect URI. Note the client ID and client secret that the provider gives you.

  2. Install the package:

    pip install mozilla-django-oidc
  1. Add the app to INSTALLED_APPS, after django.contrib.auth:
    # settings.py

    INSTALLED_APPS = [
        # ...
        'django.contrib.auth',
        'mozilla_django_oidc',
        # ...
    ]
  1. Add the authentication backend. Keep Django's ModelBackend if you still want local password login, for example for the superuser:
    # settings.py

    AUTHENTICATION_BACKENDS = [
        'mozilla_django_oidc.auth.OIDCAuthenticationBackend',
        'django.contrib.auth.backends.ModelBackend',  # Optional: keeps local password login.
    ]
  1. Add the provider settings. Read the client ID and secret from the environment or a secrets manager; don't hardcode them. Look up the endpoint URLs in your provider's documentation.
    # settings.py
    import os

    OIDC_RP_CLIENT_ID = os.environ['OIDC_RP_CLIENT_ID']
    OIDC_RP_CLIENT_SECRET = os.environ['OIDC_RP_CLIENT_SECRET']

    OIDC_OP_AUTHORIZATION_ENDPOINT = '<authorization endpoint URL>'
    OIDC_OP_TOKEN_ENDPOINT = '<token endpoint URL>'
    OIDC_OP_USER_ENDPOINT = '<userinfo endpoint URL>'

Most providers sign tokens with RS256. If yours does, also set:

    OIDC_RP_SIGN_ALGO = 'RS256'
    OIDC_OP_JWKS_ENDPOINT = '<JWKS endpoint URL>'
  1. Add the OIDC URLs to urls.py, and switch the login view to DDM's OIDC login template, which shows a login button instead of a password form:
    # urls.py

    urlpatterns = [
        # ...
        path('oidc/', include('mozilla_django_oidc.urls')),
        path('login/', auth_views.LoginView.as_view(template_name='ddm_auth/login_oidc.html'), name='ddm_login'),
        # ...
    ]
  1. Optional: Enable session refresh. To re-check users with the provider when their token expires, add the middleware after Django's session and authentication middleware:
    # settings.py

    MIDDLEWARE = [
        # ...
        'django.contrib.sessions.middleware.SessionMiddleware',
        'django.contrib.auth.middleware.AuthenticationMiddleware',
        'mozilla_django_oidc.middleware.SessionRefresh',
        # ...
    ]

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
No built-in multi-factor authentication

DDM doesn't provide multi-factor authentication (MFA) for local password login. To require MFA, enforce it at your OIDC provider (recommended) or add a third-party Django MFA package.

API access uses project tokens, not logins

The settings on this page control access to the researcher interface. The researcher API uses separate per-project access tokens that researchers create within their project. See Researchers → APIs.

docs.title: Documentation for Developers
docs.text: This section of the documentation is targeted at people who contribute to the development of DDM or who want to learn more about its development in general.

docs.title: Repository Layout
docs.text:
ddm is a reusable Django app library, split into focused sub-apps under ddm/:

Sub-app What it holds ddm.projects The DonationProject model and the researcher-facing Project Hub. ddm.datadonation Upload blueprints and extraction/processing-rule configuration. ddm.questionnaire The built-in survey tool — questions, items, filters. ddm.participation The participant-facing flow (briefing → donation → questionnaire → debriefing) and its views/models. ddm.auth Researcher authentication and permissions (ResearchProfile, ProjectAccessToken). ddm.apis The REST API researchers can use to pull their project's data programmatically. ddm.logging Exception and event logging (ExceptionLogEntry, EventLogEntry). ddm.core Shared utilities, templates, and static assets (CKEditor integration, HTML sanitization, color and template-rendering helpers) used by the apps above. ddm.encryption Field-level encryption helpers — see Topics → Encryption.

ddm.apis and ddm.encryption define no models of their own, so unlike the others they aren't listed in INSTALLED_APPS.

Two other top-level directories round out the repository:

  • test_project/ — the Django project that hosts ddm for local development and testing. It is a development harness, not a deployment reference; see Administrators → Installation Guide for how to actually configure a production Django project around ddm.
  • frontend/ — two independent Vue 3 + TypeScript applications, DDMUploader (the data donation/upload widget) and DDMQuestionnaire (the survey widget), each with its own package.json. Both are built with webpack and served into Django via django-webpack-loader. See Vue Integration below.

docs.title: Local Project for Development and Testing
docs.text: The repository includes a Django test project that can be used for local development and testing.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Development uses uv to manage the Python interpreter, virtual environment, and dependencies. Install it first — see the official installation instructions. uv itself picks up the Python version from the repository's .python-version file (currently 3.12); it will download that interpreter automatically if you don't already have it.

docs.title: Install required packages
docs.text:
Once you have cloned or forked the GitHub repository, run:

uv sync --group dev

This creates (or updates) a .venv in the repository root and installs the base runtime dependencies plus the dev dependency group (test/lint tooling) as pinned in uv.lock. There's no separate python -m venv step — uv sync manages the virtual environment for you. If you also want to build the documentation locally, add the docs group: uv sync --group dev --group docs. If you need to test against MySQL (not just the SQLite default), see Release Process → Local setup for testing against MySQL.

docs.title: Install pre-commit hooks
docs.text:
uv run pre-commit install
uv run pre-commit install --hook-type pre-push   # enables pip-audit on push

The second command matters: the pip-audit hook in .pre-commit-config.yaml is pinned to the pre-push stage, so it won't run at all unless you also install hooks for that stage specifically.

docs.title: Configure local settings
docs.text:
test_project/settings.py loads a .env file (via python-dotenv) if one exists at the repository root. By default (no .env), the test project uses SQLite at ddmtestdb, an empty SECRET_KEY, and DDM_STRICT_CSP off. Create a .env at the repository root to override any of:

DB_ENGINE=django.db.backends.sqlite3
DB_NAME=ddmtestdb
DB_USER=ddmtestuser
DB_PASSWORD=
DB_HOST=127.0.0.1
DB_PORT=
SECRET_KEY=
DDM_STRICT_CSP=

.env is git-ignored — never commit it; it's meant for your own local overrides (e.g. pointing at a local MySQL instance, or setting a real SECRET_KEY to test encryption behavior that depends on it).

Prefix the regular Django commands below with uv run so they execute inside the project's managed virtual environment.

docs.title: Run Development Server
docs.text: uv run python test_project/manage.py runserver

docs.title: Create Database Migrations
docs.text:
To create new migrations based on the changes made to the models, run:

uv run python test_project/manage.py makemigrations

docs.title: Apply migrations
docs.text: uv run python test_project/manage.py migrate

docs.title: Run Unit Tests
docs.text:
uv run python test_project/manage.py test ddm

Run a single app's tests (faster while iterating) by narrowing the target, e.g. uv run python test_project/manage.py test ddm.core.

docs.title: Code style & checks
docs.text:
Ruff (lint + format) and djLint (Django template lint) run automatically via pre-commit. Ruff is a dev dependency, so it can also be run directly:

uv run ruff check .          # lint
uv run ruff format .         # format

djLint is not a project dependency — pre-commit runs it in its own isolated environment, so uv run djlint won't work. Run it standalone with uvx, pinned to the same version pre-commit uses (v1.36.4 in .pre-commit-config.yaml at the time of writing):

uvx djlint==1.36.4 ddm --check

To run the same dependency-vulnerability scan the pip-audit pre-push hook runs, without pushing:

uv export --no-hashes --no-emit-project --group dev -o /tmp/ddm-deps.txt
uv run pip-audit -r /tmp/ddm-deps.txt

A [tool.coverage] configuration (80% minimum, ddm/** only) is set up in pyproject.toml for local use with coverage run/coverage report, but it isn't currently wired into CI, and running it as configured requires the django_coverage_plugin package, which isn't in the dev dependency group yet — add it yourself (uv add --group dev django_coverage_plugin) if you want to use it locally.

docs.title: Sass Compilation
docs.text:
To compile the scss file, sass is used. This is a separate, Node-based toolchain — independent of the Python/uv setup above.

npm install
npm run sass:watch  # run the watcher during development
npm run sass:build  # build the compressed file for distribution

docs.title: Vue Integration (Frontend)
docs.text: frontend/DDMUploader and frontend/DDMQuestionnaire are two separate Vue 3 + TypeScript projects — each has its own package.json, its own .node-version (currently v20.18.0 for both), and must be installed/run independently. Everything below applies to each one; just cd into the one you're working on.

docs.title: Development
docs.text:
First, install the Node.js version pinned in that project's .node-version (e.g. with nvm: nvm install from inside the project directory). Then install dependencies:

npm install

To run the app in development mode, serve both the webpack dev server and Django's dev server at the same time. From the project directory:

npm run serve

And, in a separate terminal from the repository root, the Django dev server:

uv run python test_project/manage.py runserver

Open your locally hosted Django app in a browser (e.g. http://localhost:8000). Changes to the Vue code trigger an automatic reload in the browser.

docs.title: Lint and test
docs.text:
npm run lint   # eslint --ext .ts,.vue src
npm run test   # vitest

docs.title: Production build
docs.text:
When it's time to deploy, or to stop running the dev server, cancel npm run serve and build the production bundle instead:

npm run build

The optimized bundles are written into the Django static file locations under ddm/core/static/, and the corresponding webpack-stats.json is updated so django-webpack-loader picks up the new build.

docs.title: Dependency updates
docs.text:
npm audit            # check for vulnerabilities
npm audit fix         # fix what can be fixed automatically
npm outdated          # check for outdated packages
npm install <package> # update one package deliberately
npm run lint && npm run test && npm run build  # verify nothing broke

Repeat for the other frontend project — updates are independent per project.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text:
• Branches: develop is the integration branch; day-to-day work and PRs target it. main only ever receives merges from develop via the release pipeline (see Release Process) — don't push or PR directly to main.
  • Before opening a PR: make sure uv run pre-commit run --all-files is clean, the test suite passes (uv run python test_project/manage.py test ddm), and — if your change touches user-facing behavior — CHANGELOG.md's current unreleased entry has a bullet describing it (see Changelog Conventions).
  • Docs: if you change anything under docs/, mkdocs.yml, pyproject.toml, or uv.lock, docs-check.yml will build the site with mkdocs build --strict on your PR — fix any broken link or nav entry it reports before merging.

docs.title: CI/CD and Releases
docs.text: This project uses GitHub Actions for testing and release automation; every workflow installs dependencies with uv sync from the committed uv.lock, so CI uses exactly the same resolved dependency versions as local development. For the full release procedure — regular releases, pre-releases, and what triggers what — see Topics → Release Process.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text: This documentation is written in Markdown and built with MkDocs + Material for MkDocs. See Topics → Documentation for how to build it locally, how it is published, and how to regenerate the screenshots.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text: CHANGELOG.md (repository root) follows these conventions, in place since February 2026 (entries from before that date may not match exactly).

docs.title: Headings
docs.text:
Each released version gets its own heading: ## X.Y.Z - YYYY-MM-DD.

The topmost entry, for the version currently in development on develop, is the one exception: it uses a single # instead of ##, has no date, and its bullets carry no commit links yet (e.g. the current # 3.0.0 entry at the top of the file). Give it a proper ## X.Y.Z - YYYY-MM-DD heading and backfill the commit links only once that version is actually released.

docs.title: Sections
docs.text:
Use any of the following ### sections that apply, in this order:

  • Fixed
  • Added
  • Changed
  • Deprecated
  • Removed
  • Technical
  • Security
  • Documentation
  • Update Guide / Migration Guide

Fixed, Added, and Changed are written for a broad audience (researchers, administrators); the rest are for a more technical audience and can assume developer knowledge.

Within Changed (and similarly for other sections, if a release touches many areas), bullets can be grouped under a #### *Area* sub-heading, e.g. #### *Uploader (data donation interface)*, #### *Questionnaire*, #### *General*.

Update Guide vs. Migration Guide — both describe what a site operator needs to do after upgrading, but at different weights: use Update Guide for a short, one-off action (e.g. "run python manage.py collectstatic"); use Migration Guide when a breaking change requires step-by-step instructions, such as a settings key that changed shape. Don't use both for the same release unless the release genuinely has both kinds of follow-up.

docs.title: Commit references
docs.text:
Every bullet should link back to the commit(s) it describes, as [`shortsha`](https://github.com/uzh/ddm/commit/shortsha), e.g.:

- **File re-upload**: Clicking re-upload now opens file dialog directly (reduced from 2 clicks)
  ([`9ad0c39`](https://github.com/uzh/ddm/commit/9ad0c39)).

Multiple commits for one bullet are comma-separated, each with its own link.

docs.title: Worked example
docs.text:
## 2.1.6 - 2025-11-19

### Fixed

- **Instruction deletion error**: Fixed crash when deleting instructions by removing reference
  to non-existent 'name' attribute ([`e12d104`](https://github.com/uzh/ddm/commit/e12d104)).
- **Upload failure modal**: Issue modal now displays correctly when all file uploads fail
  ([`d6577bd`](https://github.com/uzh/ddm/commit/d6577bd)).

### Changed

#### *General*

- **Translations**: Minor corrections to French and Italian translations
  ([`7ae9cb9`](https://github.com/uzh/ddm/commit/7ae9cb9)).

#### *Uploader (data donation interface)*

- **File re-upload**: Clicking re-upload now opens file dialog directly (reduced from 2 clicks)
  ([`9ad0c39`](https://github.com/uzh/ddm/commit/9ad0c39)).

### Update Guide

Run `python manage.py collectstatic` after upgrading to DDM v2.1.6 from the previous version.

See CHANGELOG.md itself for more real examples, including a ### Migration Guide entry (the 2.1.0 entry, for a WEBPACK_LOADER settings change).

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text: All documentation lives in the docs/ folder and is written in Markdown, built with MkDocs and the Material for MkDocs theme. Versioned deployments to GitHub Pages are managed with mike.

docs.title: Building the documentation locally
docs.text:
uv sync --group docs
uv run mkdocs serve

mkdocs serve starts a live-reloading preview at http://127.0.0.1:8000/.

mkdocs build --strict produces the static site in site/ and fails the build on broken internal links (or pages missing from the navigation), so run it before opening a pull request. CI runs the same check in .github/workflows/docs-check.yml.

The site configuration is in mkdocs.yml at the repository root — theme, navigation, Markdown extensions and plugins.

docs.title: How it is published
docs.text:
.github/workflows/publish-docs.yml is a reusable workflow that runs mike deploy --push <version> [alias]:

  • a push to develop publishes the dev version;
  • a vX.Y.Z tag publishes the X.Y version and moves the latest alias.

mike writes each version into its own subdirectory of the gh-pages branch and maintains the version selector shown at the top of the site. Documentation for releases older than the MkDocs migration is kept as a frozen archive under https://uzh.github.io/ddm/ddm/… (see Older Versions).

docs.title: Updating screenshots
docs.text:
The screenshots under docs/**/img/ are generated by tools/screenshots/update_screenshots.py (Selenium + Firefox). It logs into a local DDM instance, walks the researcher and participant flows against a fixed demo project, and captures specific page elements.

Requirements: uv sync --group dev installs selenium and webdriver_manager; Firefox must be installed (Selenium Manager fetches geckodriver automatically).

# 1. serve the demo project
uv run python test_project/manage.py runserver

# 2. regenerate the screenshots
uv run python tools/screenshots/update_screenshots.py

The demo project is referenced by the PROJECT_ID / PROJECT_SLUG / FILE_UPLOADER_ID constants at the top of the script and must already exist in the local database, together with a takeout-demo.zip fixture next to the script. Useful environment variables:

  • DDM_HEADLESS=1 — run Firefox headless.
  • DDM_SCREENSHOT_DIR=<path> — write to a scratch directory instead of docs/**/img/.

docs.title: Data Encryption
docs.text: This page describes the encryption DDM implements itself, and the encryption a site hosting DDM is responsible for setting up around it.

docs.title: Encryption in transit and at rest
Encryption in transit
docs.text: Setting up transport encryption (TLS/HTTPS for all traffic between clients and the server) is the hosting site's responsibility — see the Django deployment checklist for pointers. DDM minimizes how much donated data ever has to travel over the network in the first place by doing extraction and filtering client-side, in the participant's browser, before anything is submitted. The connection between the application server and the database should also be secured, and the database itself should live on an encrypted disk.

docs.title: Encryption at rest
docs.text:
DDM encrypts all donated data at the field level before it is written to the database. Two models hold encrypted data — DataDonation and QuestionnaireResponse (both inherit from ModelWithEncryptedData, ddm/encryption/models.py) — and both encrypt/decrypt through their owning DonationProject.

Each DonationProject has its own RSA keypair. The public key is used to encrypt data on write; the private key is needed to decrypt it. How that keypair is obtained depends on the project:

  • Standard projects (super_secret=False, the default): on first save, DDM generates a genuinely random RSA-2048 keypair (RSA.generate(2048), no seed). The public key is stored as-is in DonationProject.public_key; the private key is wrapped at rest (see below) using a key derived from settings.SECRET_KEY, and the wrapped bytes are stored in DonationProject.wrapped_private_key. Decryption unwraps this field with SECRET_KEY — nothing needs to be re-derived or remembered per project.
  • Enhanced-encryption ("super secret") projects (super_secret=True, the "Enable enhanced encryption" checkbox researchers see at project creation, ddm/projects/templates/ddm_projects/form_sections/_enhanced_encryption_block.html): the keypair is never stored. Instead it is deterministically re-derived on every use from a project-specific passphrase (held only in memory, via the DonationProject.secret/ secret_key property — never persisted to the database) and the project's salt. Losing the passphrase means the data can never be decrypted again, by design. Because the passphrase isn't in the database, it also can't be used server-side to template donated data into follow-up questionnaire questions (get_decrypted_data needs the real passphrase, not SECRET_KEY).
  • Legacy projects: any standard project created before wrapped_private_key existed falls back to the same on-the-fly derivation as enhanced-encryption projects, keyed on settings.SECRET_KEY instead of a per-project passphrase. This keeps already-encrypted data for those projects decryptable without a backfill migration.

All three cases share one salt per project: DonationProject.get_salt() simply returns str(self.date_created) — the project's creation timestamp, not an independently generated random value. date_created must not be changed after creation, or the legacy/enhanced derivation paths stop reproducing the original keypair.

SECRET_KEY is part of your encryption key material

For every standard project, settings.SECRET_KEY is what the private key is wrapped with. Losing SECRET_KEY (and not having a backup) makes every standard project's donated data permanently undecryptable; leaking it, combined with database access, lets an attacker decrypt everything. Treat it accordingly — see Administrators → Security.

The branching logic above lives in DonationProject.get_decryptor() (ddm/projects/models.py); _generate_and_store_keypair() is only ever called once, from save()'s "no public_key yet" branch.

docs.title: Encryption and decryption process
docs.text:
DDM uses hybrid asymmetric/symmetric encryption for the data itself (RSA key sizes alone can't hold more than a small amount of data, so each payload is encrypted symmetrically and only the symmetric key is wrapped asymmetrically). This part of the scheme — implemented in the Encryption/Decryption classes in ddm/encryption/models.py — is unchanged by the private-key storage change described above; what changed is only where the private key used in step 2 of decryption comes from.

Encrypting a value (Encryption.encrypt()):

  1. Generate a random 128-bit AES session key, unique to this one value.
  2. Encrypt the value symmetrically with that session key, using AES in EAX mode (authenticated encryption — this also produces a verification tag).
  3. Encrypt the session key asymmetrically with the project's RSA public key, using PKCS#1 OAEP padding.
  4. Concatenate encrypted_session_key + nonce + tag + ciphertext, base64-encode it, and store that as the field's value.

Decrypting a value (Decryption.decrypt()):

  1. Obtain the project's RSA private key — via get_decryptor()'s three-way branch described above.
  2. Split the stored, base64-decoded payload back into encrypted_session_key, nonce, tag, and ciphertext.
  3. Decrypt the session key asymmetrically with the private key (PKCS#1 OAEP).
  4. Decrypt the ciphertext symmetrically with the session key (AES-EAX), verifying the tag.

docs.title: Deriving a keypair from a passphrase (enhanced-encryption and legacy projects)
docs.text:
When a keypair must be re-derived from a passphrase rather than read from storage (AsyncSyncCrypto.get_rsa()):

  1. Compute a 128-bit HMAC digest of passphrase + salt (no hash function parameter is passed to pycryptodome's HMAC.new(), so it defaults to MD5 — this is used purely as a seed, not for its cryptographic properties).
  2. Use that digest to seed a custom deterministic PRNG (PRNG in ddm/encryption/models.py, itself built from repeated HMAC calls over an incrementing counter).
  3. Generate the RSA-2048 keypair using that PRNG as the randomness source (RSA.generate(2048, randfunc=PRNG(seed))) — the same seed always yields the same keypair.

The public key is exported and stored normally; the private key is never persisted for these projects and must be re-derived the same way on every decryption.

docs.title: Wrapping a standard project's private key
docs.text:
For a standard project, the randomly generated private key is protected at rest with a second, independent layer of AES-EAX encryption (wrap_private_key()/unwrap_private_key() and _derive_wrap_key() in ddm/encryption/models.py):

  1. Derive a 256-bit AES key from settings.SECRET_KEY via HKDF-SHA256, using a fixed, non-secret domain-separation context string (b"ddm:donationproject:private-key-wrap:v1") — this key is the same for every project on a given deployment, since it depends only on SECRET_KEY.
  2. Encrypt the DER-encoded private key with AES-EAX, using a fresh random nonce for this project (never a deterministic one — that would make the per-project wrap key reuse unsafe).
  3. Store nonce + tag + ciphertext in DonationProject.wrapped_private_key.

Unwrapping reverses this and raises ValueError if SECRET_KEY is wrong or the stored bytes were tampered with (the AES-EAX tag won't verify).

docs.title: Internationalization
docs.text:
The researcher-facing Project Hub interface currently only supports English.

The participant-facing interface (briefing/donation/questionnaire/debriefing) currently supports English, German, Italian, and French.

docs.title: Language Detection
docs.text: The language in which the interface for participants is displayed is determined by the default language of the participant's browser. If a language is not implemented for the participant interface, it falls back to English.

docs.title: Adding Support for a New Language
docs.text: Supporting a new language means adding translations in two separate places: the Django-rendered parts of the participant flow, and the two Vue applications.

docs.title: Django Components
docs.text:
Only ddm.participation currently ships translations, at ddm/participation/locale/:

ddm/participation/locale/
├── de/LC_MESSAGES/django.po
├── fr/LC_MESSAGES/django.po
└── it/LC_MESSAGES/django.po

(There is no en/ directory — English is LANGUAGE_CODE in test_project/settings.py, so it's the fallback/source language rather than a translated catalog.)

See the Django i18n docs for the full picture. To add or update a locale:

cd ddm/participation
uv run --project ../.. django-admin makemessages -l de

-l de is the locale you want to create or update (de, fr, it, or a new one). This creates/updates ddm/participation/locale/<locale>/LC_MESSAGES/django.po — add or edit translations there. Then compile it to the .mo file gettext actually reads at runtime:

uv run --project ../.. django-admin compilemessages

The other ddm.* sub-apps (ddm.apis, ddm.auth, ddm.core, ddm.datadonation, ddm.logging, ddm.projects, ddm.questionnaire) each already wrap their AppConfig.verbose_name in gettext_lazy (_()), but none of them ship a locale/ directory yet — translating the researcher-facing admin interface would mean adding one per app and marking up the rest of each app's user-facing strings.

docs.title: Vue Components
docs.text:
Each Vue app manages its own translations with vue-i18n, as plain JSON files under its own src/locales/:

frontend/DDMUploader/src/locales/{en,de,fr,it}.json
frontend/DDMQuestionnaire/src/locales/{en,de,fr,it}.json

To add a new language, add the locale as a new top-level key to both apps' JSON files (the Uploader and the Questionnaire are independent projects with independent translation files — see For Developers → Vue Integration) and fill in a translation for every key already present for the other locales.

Don't edit the built copy

ddm/core/static/ddm_core/frontend/uploader/locale/*.json looks identical to frontend/DDMUploader/src/locales/*.json, but it's a build artifact — webpack copies it there from the source files whenever you run npm run build (see Vue Integration). Edit the source files under frontend/*/src/locales/, never the copy under ddm/core/static/; your changes will be overwritten by the next build otherwise.

New translation keys only reach the served frontend after a rebuild (npm run build, or while npm run serve is running during development).

docs.title: Release Process
docs.text: This project is versioned with a single, static version field in pyproject.toml — there is no automatic version bump anywhere. Which CI pipeline runs is decided purely by the prefix of the git tag you push, independent of what the version string itself looks like. Keep that in mind: a v-prefixed tag always merges develop into main and re-points the docs latest alias, even if the version itself is a beta (e.g. v3.0.0b5) — only a pre-prefixed tag skips that. Double-check the prefix before pushing.

docs.title: Regular release (vX.Y.Z)
docs.text:
Run these from a clean develop checkout, in order:

uv version X.Y.Z

This writes X.Y.Z into pyproject.toml's version field and re-locks uv.lock.

git add pyproject.toml uv.lock

Also update CHANGELOG.md: promote the version's entry from the single-# placeholder used during development to a proper ## X.Y.Z - YYYY-MM-DD heading, and backfill its commit links (see Changelog Conventions), then:

git add CHANGELOG.md
git commit -m "chore: bump version to vX.Y.Z"
git push origin develop

Tag the commit you just pushed and push the tag — the tag must start with v and must match the version you just set exactly:

git tag vX.Y.Z
git push origin vX.Y.Z

Pushing that tag triggers .github/workflows/merge-dev-to-main.yml, which:

  1. Runs the full test matrix (test-ddm.yml: Python 3.12 and 3.14, SQLite and MySQL).
  2. If tests pass, publishes the docs under version X.Y (minor only, e.g. 3.0 from v3.0.4) via publish-docs.yml, and moves the latest alias to point at it.
  3. Merges develop into main (everlytic/branch-merge, commit message [Automated] Merged develop into target main).

The push to main created by that merge then triggers .github/workflows/publish-to-pypi.yml, which runs the tests again (MySQL only) and, if they pass, runs uv build followed by uv publish — authenticated via PyPI Trusted Publishing (OIDC), no API token involved.

If the tagged build fails: delete the tag, fix the problem, and re-tag. Do not reuse a tag name for different content once it's been pushed:

git tag -d vX.Y.Z
git push origin --delete vX.Y.Z
# fix the problem, commit, push to develop again, then:
git tag vX.Y.Z
git push origin vX.Y.Z

docs.title: Pre-release (preX.Y.Zb<n>)
docs.text:
Use this for a beta/RC you want on PyPI and in the dev docs without touching main or the latest docs alias.

uv version X.Y.ZbN   # PEP 440 pre-release, e.g. 3.0.0b5
git add pyproject.toml uv.lock
git commit -m "chore: bump version to preX.Y.ZbN"
git push origin develop

Tag with a pre-prefixed tag (not v!) — the exact suffix only needs to start with pre, but keep it matching the version for clarity:

git tag preX.Y.ZbN
git push origin preX.Y.ZbN

Pushing a pre* tag triggers .github/workflows/publish-prerelease-to-pypi.yml, which:

  1. Runs the test matrix against MySQL only.
  2. Publishes the docs as the dev version (title "dev (develop)") — not latest.
  3. Runs uv build + uv publish.

develop is never merged into main by this path.

docs.title: Other triggers
docs.text:
• Plain push to develop (no tag): runs the test matrix (test-develop.yml) and republishes the dev docs version — no PyPI publish.
  • Dependabot PR: dependabot-merge.yml auto-approves and merges a dependency-bump PR that Dependabot itself already opened; it doesn't update any dependencies on its own, and merging it into main triggers publish-to-pypi.yml like any other push to main.
  • PR touching docs/**, mkdocs.yml, pyproject.toml, or uv.lock: docs-check.yml runs uv sync --group docs && uv run mkdocs build --strict as a merge gate — it fails the PR if any internal link is broken or a page is missing from the nav. It does not deploy anything.

docs.title: Local setup for testing against MySQL
docs.text:
The CI matrix above includes MySQL; to reproduce that locally you need the db-drivers group, which needs the MySQL client headers installed first (mysqlclient compiles against them):

# macOS:
brew install mysql-client pkg-config
export PKG_CONFIG_PATH="$(brew --prefix mysql-client)/lib/pkgconfig"

# Debian/Ubuntu:
sudo apt-get install default-libmysqlclient-dev pkg-config

uv sync --group dev --group db-drivers

docs.title: Researchers
docs.text: Use this section to set up a data donation project with DDM, collect donations, and download the data.

docs.title: How DDM Works
docs.text: DDM has two parts: the Researcher Interface, where you set up and manage your projects, and the Participation Interface, which your participants go through.

docs.title: Researcher Interface
docs.text: In the Researcher Interface, you create projects, configure what participants see, and download the collected data. You configure each project from its Project Hub:

docs.title: Participation Interface
docs.text:
Every participant goes through the briefing page, data donation, and debriefing page; the questionnaire step is optional. These steps run in order and can't be skipped or reordered.

  1. Briefing page: Participants learn about your study. You can require participants to explicitly confirm their consent to take part before they continue.

  2. Data donation: Participants follow your instructions to request their data from a platform and upload the file. DDM extracts and filters the data in the participant's browser - no personal data reaches your server until the participant reviews the extracted data and explicitly consents to donating it.

  3. Questionnaire (optional): Participants answer your questions, which can refer to their donated data.

  4. Debriefing page: Participants see a closing message, for example a thank-you note or a link back to your survey.

docs.title: Where to Start
docs.text:
1. Create a project.
  2. Configure the data collection: briefing, data donation, questionnaire, and debriefing.
  3. Test and launch your project before you share it with participants.
  4. Download the collected data.

docs.title: Project List
docs.text:
When you open DDM, you see a list of all your projects:

To create a project, click Create New Project.

docs.title: Set Up a New Project
docs.text: Enter the project's name, URL identifier, contact information, and data protection statement. For what each field means, see General Project Settings → Public Information. You can change all of these later.

docs.title: Advanced Options: Enhanced Encryption
docs.text:
DDM encrypts all collected data. By default, DDM can decrypt the data itself, so you can view and download it without extra steps.

With Enable enhanced encryption, you set a project password when you create the project. Donations and questionnaire responses can only be decrypted with this password. DDM doesn't store it, so nobody without the password can read the data, including the administrators of your DDM server. You'll need to enter the password whenever you download data, both in the Data Center and through the API.

Consider enhanced encryption if your data protection requirements say that only your research team may be able to read the data.

Before you enable enhanced encryption

  • You can't change it later. Enhanced encryption can't be turned on or off after you create the project.
  • If you lose the password, you lose the data. The password can't be recovered or reset. Store it in a password manager and share it with your team.
  • Some features aren't available. You can't refer to donated data in your questionnaire (see Data Integration).

For technical details, see Developers → Encryption.

docs.title: After Creating the Project
docs.text: Click Create Project. DDM opens the Project Hub of your new project.

docs.title: Delete a Project or Data
docs.text: The Project Hub's Danger Zone section holds all options to reset or delete the data collected in a project.

docs.title: Reset Project Data
docs.text: With this option, you can delete all data collected for a given project. This removes all data donations and questionnaire responses, and also removes the participant records themselves - so the Participation Statistics (started/completed counts, etc.) reset to zero as well.

docs.title: Delete Participant
docs.text:
You can delete the data for a specific participant by providing their external participation id.

Tip

You can show your participants their external participation id during the study (e.g., embedded in a text block as part of the questionnaire or on the debriefing page) and inform them that by providing this ID they can request the deletion of their data in the future if they change their mind.

This function can then help you to delete a participant from the database (if your study is still ongoing at the time a participant requests the deletion of their data).

docs.title: Delete Project
docs.text: With this option you can delete the current project including all its components (e.g., Uploaders, Blueprints, Instructions, Questions etc.). This will also delete all associated data.

docs.title: Export & Copy
docs.text:
Reuse a project's configuration - its file uploaders, blueprints, and questionnaire - for a new study, instead of rebuilding it from scratch. Collected data is never included in either action.

You can access these options in Project Hub > Export & Copy.

docs.title: Copy a Project
docs.text: Click Copy Project to duplicate the project - including all its uploaders, blueprints, and questions - into a brand-new project. Review the suggested name and URL identifier (DDM proposes <name> (copy) and <slug>-copy) before confirming.

docs.title: Export a Project
docs.text: Click Export Project to download the project's configuration as a JSON file.

docs.title: Import a Project
docs.text:
From your project list, click Import Project, upload a previously exported JSON file, then review and confirm the new project's name and URL identifier.

Moving a project between DDM instances

Export and import together let you move a project's configuration to a different DDM instance - for example, from a test/staging server to your production server.

docs.title: General Project Settings
docs.text:
The general project settings have four sections:

Section What it's for Public Information What participants see about your project, such as its name and your contact details, and whether the project is active. URL Parameter Extraction Save information that's passed in the participation link, such as a participant ID from your survey tool. Redirect Configuration Send participants to another website at the end, such as a follow-up survey. Branding Your colors and logos in the Participation Interface.

docs.title: Public Information
docs.text:
This information is visible to participants and helps them understand and trust your study.

Settings

Project Name

The project name shown in the participant's browser tab.

URL Identifier

The part of the participation link that identifies your project. For example, with my-study, participants take part at https://your-ddm-server/ddm/my-study/briefing.

You can use letters, numbers, hyphens (-), and underscores (_).

Active

Whether participants can take part. While a project is inactive, participants who open the link see a page saying that participation isn't possible at the moment.

Contact Information

Contact details of the researcher responsible for the project. Participants can open them from the footer at every step, so they know who runs the study and how to reach you.

Data Protection Statement

How you process the collected data. Participants can open it from the footer at every step.

docs.title: URL Parameter Extraction
docs.text:
A link can carry extra information after a question mark, called URL parameters. For example, in https://your-ddm-server/ddm/my-study/briefing?participant=ID123, the parameter participant has the value ID123. DDM can save these values for each participant.

This is useful for:

  • Linking DDM to other tools. If participants come from a survey tool (for example, SoSciSurvey or Qualtrics) or a recruitment partner, pass their ID in the link (?participant=ID123). You can then match the donated data to their survey responses.
  • Tracking recruitment channels. Use a different link for each channel (for example, ?channel=email and ?channel=social-media) to see where participants came from.

Settings

URL parameter extraction enabled

Whether DDM saves URL parameters. If enabled, DDM saves them when a participant opens the briefing page.

Expected URL parameter

The names of the parameters to save. Separate multiple names with semicolons, for example participant;channel.

The values are saved for each participant and included in the data download. If a parameter is missing from the link, the value is empty (shown as an empty cell or null, depending on the program you open the file with). DDM ignores all other parameters.

docs.title: Redirect Configuration
docs.text:
At the end of the study, DDM can show participants a button on the debriefing page that takes them to another website.

This is useful for:

  • Linking DDM to other tools. Send participants to a follow-up survey (for example, in SoSciSurvey or Qualtrics) or back to a recruitment partner, and pass their ID in the link (see below).
  • Linking to your project website.

Settings

Redirect enabled

Whether the debriefing page shows a button that links to the Redirect address.

Redirect address

The URL the button links to. Required if Redirect enabled is on.

Pass information in the redirect link

The URL can include variables that DDM fills in for each participant:

  • {{ participant_id }}: The participant's ID.
  • {{ project_id }}: The project's ID.
  • {{ url_parameter.<name> }}: The value of an extracted URL parameter, for example {{ url_parameter.participant }}.

For example, to send participants back to your survey with the ID they arrived with: https://survey.example.org?participant={{ url_parameter.participant }}

For all available variables, see Template Rendering.

docs.title: Branding
docs.text:
Customize how the Participation Interface looks: set its colors and add up to two logos.

Settings

Show project title

Whether the project title is shown in the header.

Primary Color

The color of buttons and highlights. DDM creates lighter and darker shades from it automatically. Choose a dark color so that button text stays readable.

Background Color

The background color of all pages. Choose a very light color.

Header Image Left and Header Image Right

Images shown on the left and right side of the header, for example your institution's or project's logo. Use a JPEG or PNG file. SVG files aren't supported.

docs.title: Project Hub
docs.text:
Each project has a Project Hub: the page where you configure the project, share it with participants, and access the collected data.

The Project Hub has these areas:

  • Overview: The project's name, ID, and status (active or inactive), the participation link to share with participants, and a test link to try the project yourself.
  • General Project Settings: The project's name, contact information, data protection statement, and other basic settings. See General Project Settings.
  • Data Collection Configuration: What participants see at each step: briefing, data donation, questionnaire, and debriefing. See Data Collection Configuration.
  • Data Center: Download the collected data and view participation statistics. See Data Center.
  • Project Logs: Events and errors in your project, for example failed uploads. See Project Logs.
  • Export & Copy: Copy the project or export its configuration, for example to reuse it in a new study. See Export & Copy.
  • Danger Zone: Delete the project, all collected data, or the data of individual participants. See Delete a Project or Data.

docs.title: Test and Launch
docs.text: Before sharing your project with real participants, try it out yourself using the Test Link, then launch it once everything looks right.

docs.title: The Test Link
docs.text:
While setting up your project, use the Test Link (in the Project Hub) to try it out, not the participation link.

The participation link remembers you, so you can only take part once (or always open it in an incognito tab). Each time you open it, you have to go through the whole study from the start, even if you only want to check one part, like the questionnaire. Your test answers would also be mixed in with those of real participants.

The Test Link avoids both problems: you can try out your project as often as you like, and your test runs are clearly marked as tests.

Each project has its own Test Link, shown next to the regular Participant Link in the Project Hub's Overview section. It looks like your participant link with a test parameter appended, e.g.:

https://your-domain.com/project-slug/briefing/?test=<test-token>

Opening this link enters the test mode and always starts a brand-new, flagged test run - regardless of whatever participant session your browser's cookies currently point to. There's no need to use a private/incognito window or clear cookies between test runs; just revisit the Test Link. While you're on any page of a test run, a Test Mode banner is shown at the top.

Sharing the Test Link

The token in the Test Link is a long, unguessable random string, but anyone who has the link can use it to generate test participants for your project. Only share it with people you trust to test the project with you.

docs.title: Regenerating the Test Link
docs.text:
If you've shared the link more widely than intended, click Regenerate Test Link to invalidate it. Once regenerated:

  • The old link stops working - anyone who still has it sees a "test link disabled" page instead of starting (or continuing) a run.
  • Test runs already collected under the old link are not deleted. They remain in your project's data exactly as before (see below).

docs.title: Jumping to a Specific Step or Page
docs.text:
Instead of clicking through the whole participation flow to check, say, the questionnaire, use the navigation options in the test banner - pick a step (and, for the questionnaire, a page) from the dropdowns and click Go.

Jumping between steps/pages like this keeps using the same test run (so data you've already donated in that run stays available) - it only starts a new one when you revisit the plain Test Link, or use the banner's Start new test run button.

Jumping flags the run as out of order

Reaching a step out of its normal order marks that test run accordingly - this affects whether it's included in exports by default, see below.

docs.title: Test Runs in Your Data and Exports
docs.text:
Every test run is clearly recorded as such, so it's never mistaken for a real participation. Still, a test run you completed start to finish, in order behaves like a normal participant: it's useful for checking that the whole flow and your data actually works, so it's included by default in:

  • The Participation Overview download and the Donations/Responses API (see Data Download and the APIs topic).

A test run where you used the navigation options to jump ahead, on the other hand, has incomplete or out-of-order data and isn't meaningful for analysis - these runs are excluded by default from the same exports. If you need to inspect them anyway (e.g., while debugging), the Donations and Responses API accept an include_broken_test_runs=true URL parameter to include them.

docs.title: Launch Your Project
docs.text:
Once your test runs look right:

  1. In General Project Settings → Public Information, enable Active.
  2. Share the participation link with your participants.

docs.title: Data Center
docs.text:
The Data Center is where you get the data you collected and follow your project's progress. To open it, go to the Project Hub and scroll to the Data Center section of the Project Hub.

  • Download: Download the donations and questionnaire responses.
  • Statistics: See how many people took part, donated their data, and completed the study.
  • APIs: Download data with a script, for example to update your analysis automatically while the study is running.

To check events and errors, for example failed uploads, open Project Logs in the Project Hub. See Project Logs.

Enhanced encryption

For projects with enhanced encryption, you need the project password to download data, both here and through the API.

Store downloaded data securely

Downloaded files aren't encrypted. Store them according to your data protection plan, for example on an encrypted drive that only your team can access.

docs.title: Download
docs.text:
You can download your data in two ways:

  • In the Project Hub, in the Data Center section. Described on this page.
  • Through the API, with a script. See Download Through the API.

For projects with enhanced encryption, you need the project password for every download.

docs.title: Download Donations
docs.text:
In the Project Hub, you download donations one participant at a time:

  1. In the Data Center section of the Project Hub, download the Participation Overview. It's a CSV file with one row per participant, including participants who didn't finish.

  2. In the file, open the link in the donation_download_link column of the participant. Open it in the browser in which you're logged in to DDM.

Each donation is a JSON file with the data that each Blueprint extracted, using the field names you defined under Relevant Fields.

Download all donations at once

There's no button to download all donations at once. To download the donations of all participants, use the API.

docs.title: Participation Overview
docs.text:
The Participation Overview has these columns:

Column Description participant_id The participant's ID. is_test_case True if the participant used the test link. start_time When the participant first opened the project, for example 2024-07-16 20:30:40.863581+00:00 (UTC). end_time When the participant reached the debriefing page. current_step The last step the participant reached: 0 briefing, 1 data donation, 2 questionnaire, 3 debriefing. completed True if the participant completed the study. url_parameter All extracted URL parameters in one column, if enabled, for example {"participant": "ID123", "channel": "email"}. Split it into separate columns in your analysis software. extra_data briefing_consent ("1" or "0") if you ask for consent on the briefing page. For test runs, it may also contain internal test information (see Test and Launch). donation_download_link The link to download the participant's donation.

For each Blueprint, the file has these columns, where <X> is the Blueprint's ID:

Column Description bp-<X>_name The Blueprint's name.
